How SpaceX plans to land on Mars in 2018
That's thier plan? Send a manned orbital craft on an unmanned one way trip to mars? WTF is that going to do?

Not at all. This is just another step in a long chain of events.

The ultimate goal here is colonization of Mars. And I mean genuine colonization, not a colony of a dozen astronauts and scientists - but hundreds of thousands of people developing in a self sustaining colony in parallel to Earth's development.

So the first step in this process was to get rocket prices down. That's why SpaceX has been working on things like rockets that can autonomously land themselves. The long run idea is rockets come spaceships that are little different than planes. They launch, land, and refueling and repairing they're launched again. He's already chopped tens of millions of dollars off the price of launches and he keeps pushing them lower and lower even when he's already able to undercut everybody by tens of millions of dollars. So that's been a success and is ongoing.

The next step was to develop a rocket capable of getting to Mars. It's a bit further than launching satellites into Earth orbit. That's the Falcon Heavy as mentioned in the video. It's been developed and will have its first test flight in early 2017 with its first commercial flight scheduled for March 2017.

Another step, more or less simultaneous to the first, was the development of a crew capsule that could land on Mars. That's the Dragon 2 and where the retropulsion (or in other words firing your rockets to slow yourself down instead of speed yourself up) technology came from. The payload they're going to be landing in 2018 will be 8-10x heavier than anything NASA has ever landed and that exponentially increases the complexity and challenges in landing. There's also the issue that this same capsule needs to be able to come back to Earth. It's going to be going really really fast and when it gets into the atmosphere it's going to face incinerating temperatures. Lots of technical challenges to overcome - that's a challenge that's ongoing. Several demo and testing missions are planned for the Dragon 2 for mid next year with the first commercial crew transport to the ISS expected in 2018.

And this step - actually getting to Mars is another huge part of it. Once there expect to see lots of experiments rolled out related to colonization. What they are is, for now, anybody's guess. I'd expect to see food production tests (growing potatoes in particular) to be among them.

The key step is scheduled for 2024. That is when SpaceX plans to launch the first manned mission to Mars.
